A B S T R A C T  
Thin film CdTe-based photovoltaic devices have achieved high efficiency above 22 %. The recent improvement in 
efficiency is due to Se alloying in the CdTe absorbers to form a CdSeTe/CdTe structure. The subsequent band gap 
grading increases the short circuit current density. The Se can be introduced by depositing a precursor thin film 
of either CdSe or a CdSeTe alloy and then diffusing the Se into the CdTe during the high temperature cadmium 
chloride activation process. Using CdSe is preferred because it is easier to control the Se concentration. However, 
during fabrication of the CdSeTe/CdTe devices, the CdSe thickness needs to be precisely controlled to prevent the 
retention of a CdSe remnant layer after the activation treatment. Retention of a remnant CdSe layer causes a 
dramatic reduction in device efficiency. In this work, we show that the reduction in efficiency is caused by a 
number of factors. The remnant CdSe layer is n-type which moves the position of the p-n junction. Also, it is 
widely thought that the CdSe remnants are photo-inactive. In this work, we clarify that the individual CdSe 
grains are actually highly photo-active. However, the grain sizes in the CdSe remnant and the adjacent CdSeTe 
layer are very small resulting in a high grain boundary area. Although the grain boundaries are passivated with 
chlorine, cathodoluminescence imaging and electrical measurements show that this is only partially effective. 
Also, EQE measurements show that the remnant CdSe causes parasitic absorption. Overall, the remnant CdSe 
layer causes a reduction in short circuit current density and device efficiency. The thickness of the CdSe precursor 
layer and the cadmium chloride activation process conditions must be precisely optimised to ensure that all the 
CdSe is consumed and inter-diffused to form the CdSeTe alloy for highest efficiency devices.

The Se can be introduced into the CdTe at the front of the device in 
two ways. It can be deposited as a CdSe thin film [7] or as a CdSeTe alloy 
[8]. In both cases, the Se grading is achieved by diffusion during the 
cadmium chloride (CdCl2) activation process. The use of a thin film CdSe 
layer is preferred in manufacturing because the thin film composition is 
fixed and easily reproducible. However, although CdSe alloying signif­
icantly enhances the device efficiency, its thickness needs to be precisely 
controlled to ensure the formation of the CdSeTe and avoid any 
remaining intact CdSe layer after the CdCl2 activation treatment. 
Previous studies using CdSe as an n-type window layer have shown 
that it can significantly reduce the short circuit current due to parasitic 
absorption of short wavelength photons as shown in external quantum 
efficiency (EQE) measurements [9–11]. Poplawsky et al. [9] used elec­
tron beam-induced current (EBIC) to show the CdSe window layer is 
photo-inactive in a device structure of SnO2/CdSe/CdTe. Baines et al. 
[11] also suggested that the CdSe wurtzite phase is photo-inactive 
whereas the CdTe1-xSex zinc blende structure is photo-active. Baines 
et al. [11] also investigated the CdSe residual layer in a device structure 
of FTO/CdS/CdSe/CdTe. In this device configuration, the CdS layer is 
the n-type emitter if the CdSe layer is completely alloyed in the CdTe. 
The device structure used here is FTO/intrinsic SnO2/CdSe/CdTe. The 
intrinsic SnO2 layer is the n-type emitter once the CdSe precursor is 
completely alloyed with the CdTe. It is often assumed that the intrinsic 
SnO2 layer is highly resistive. This is a misconception because it actually 
has a carrier concentration in the order of 1018~1019 cm−3 [12,13]. 
In a device with an intrinsic SnO2 emitter, it is widely thought that 
any remnant CdSe is photo-inactive. Here we show using cath­
odoluminescence on device cross-sections in transmission electron mi­
croscopy, that the thin film CdSe is highly photo-active. The problem 
with the remnant CdSe is connected to its n-type electrical behaviour 
and the small-grained nature of its hexagonal structure. With this in­
formation, we are now able to more accurately model the device 
operation. 
2. Material and methods 
Device fabrication: the CdSe/CdTe devices were deposited by 
sequentially evaporating CdSe and CdTe bilayers onto glass/FTO/SnO2 
superstrates (TEC 12D™, NSG Pilkington). The intrinsic SnO2 acts as the 
window or emitter layer. The fabrication of the CdSe/CdTe stack enables 
precise control of the Se concentration, which is more compatible with 
large-scale industrial production. The interdiffusion between CdSe and 
CdTe was achieved by a CdCl2 activation process at 400 ◦C for 30 min in 
a dry air environment. After the activation process, these devices were 
Cu doped using 0.1 mM CuCl2 solution in DI water. The Cu activation 
was carried out at 200 ◦C for 20 min in a hot oven in ambient envi­
ronment. The device fabrication and processing details have been re­
ported in more detail in a previous publication [7]. 
Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was conducted using a 
Helios G4 Xe-plasma focused ion beam (PFIB). The large cross-sectional 
region was milled at 60 nA to be scanned with a CMOS EBSD detector. 
Prior to milling, a 3 μm layer of Pt was deposited at 16 kV and 30 nA to 
protect the CdTe cross-section edge. A 36◦pre-tilt holder was used to tilt 
the cross-section edge at 54◦during ion milling and 70◦for EBSD. EBSD 
scanning was carried out at 10 kV and 6.4 nA with a step size of 20 nm. 
During EBSD scanning, the detector was set to examine for the presence 
of both hexagonal and cubic components. This enables us to evaluate

3.2. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) 
Fig. 3 shows an EBSD image of a cross-section of the CdSe/CdTe stack 
with a CdSe precursor thickness of 120 nm before the CdCl2 activation 
treatment. The CdTe grains show a columnar structure with a small 
grain size of ~500 nm in the lateral direction (Fig. 3a). The grain ori­
entations of both the CdTe and the CdSe are poorly indexed in EBSD due 
to the presence of a high density of stacking faults in both layers. Fig. 3b 
shows a phase map for the sample in which the cubic and hexagonal 
components are coloured blue and yellow, respectively. Interestingly, 
hexagonal and cubic components are identified in both the as-deposited 
CdTe and CdSe films. Additionally, the CdSe layer consists of remark­
ably small grains (<100 nm). 
After the activation treatment, the EBSD analysis in Fig. 4a shows 
that the CdSe/CdTe stack formed with the 120 nm thick CdSe precursor 
has been completely converted to the cubic phase. The CdSe layer had, 
apparently, been completely consumed during the activation treatment 
and alloyed with CdTe to form a CdSeTe alloy. The hexagonal compo­
nent in the untreated device is no longer present due to the complete 
removal of stacking faults throughout the absorber [14]. In addition, the 
CdSeTe and CdTe grains have recrystallised and grown larger during the 
activation process. The grain orientation randomises as revealed in the 
coloured IPF map shown in Fig. 4a. 
In contrast, the 400 nm thick CdSe layer was not fully consumed 
during activation and an approximately 300 nm thick CdSe layer 
remained intact. The CdSe residue has a purely wurtzite (hexagonal) 
crystal structure as depicted in yellow in the phase map shown in Fig. 4b 
and c. This is because the stacking faults have been removed during 
activation and the cubic component has been removed. The remaining 
CdSe grains are small (average grain size of ~270 nm) in comparison to 
the alloyed CdTe grains in the samples, but substantially larger than the 
as-deposited grains in the size range of < 100 nm. 
To investigate the microstructure of the remaining CdSe layer, 
Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy (STEM) and EDS measure­
ment were conducted (Fig. 5). The Cl signal in the EDS elemental maps 
clearly delineates the grain boundaries because CdCl2 diffuses along the 
grain boundaries during the activation treatment. Chlorine also deco­
rates the junction with the tin oxide window layer along the surface of 
the TEC 12D substrate. Interestingly, the adjacent CdSeTe bottom layer 
covering the CdSe remnants contains even smaller grains. This CdSeTe 
bottom layer did not completely recrystallise during the CdCl2 activa­
tion treatment. The Se signal shows that Se diffuses into the CdTe 
initially along grain boundaries and later into grain interiors to form 
CdSeTe.

4. Conclusions 
The efficiency of thin film CdTe based modules has been increased by 
adding selenium to the front of the absorber layer to create a diffused 
CdSeTe alloy layer. The preferred way of introducing the Se is by 
depositing CdSe and then inter-diffusing the layer into the CdTe layer 
above during the high temperature cadmium chloride activation pro­
cess. The thickness of the CdSe must be optimised since the device ef­
ficiency is severely reduced if not all the CdSe is consumed, and a 
remnant hexagonal n-type layer remains. 
In this study, we have used CL in STEM to show that the individual 
CdSe grains are highly photo-active following the cadmium chloride 
activation process. The grain boundaries are passivated to some degree 
by chlorine decoration in a similar way to cadmium telluride. CdSe is 
photo-inactive prior to the activation process. However, due to their 
very small grain size, the large number of grain boundaries causes severe 
carrier recombination in the remnant CdSe and in the adjacent CdSeTe 
intermediate layers. These observations are confirmed using electrical 
measurements. The CdSe remnant moves the position of the p-n junction 
in the device. A new p-n junction is formed between the n-type CdSe 
remnant and adjacent p-type CdSeTe intermediate layer. However, the 
small, grained nature of the n-type CdSe remnant and p-type interme­
diate CdSeTe layer causes parasitic absorption. This dramatically re­
duces the short circuit current density and the device efficiency. 
Therefore, the precursor CdSe thickness in the CdSe/CdTe stack must be 
precisely controlled to completely remove the CdSe remnant and elim­
inate the parasitic absorption. 
Interestingly, the band gap energy (1.7 eV) of CdSe and its high 
photo-activity make it a promising top cell in a silicon-based tandem 
photovoltaic device.

4. Conclusions 
The efficiency of thin film CdTe based modules has been increased by 
adding selenium to the front of the absorber layer to create a diffused 
CdSeTe alloy layer. The preferred way of introducing the Se is by 
depositing CdSe and then inter-diffusing the layer into the CdTe layer 
above during the high temperature cadmium chloride activation pro-
cess. The thickness of the CdSe must be optimised since the device ef-
ficiency is severely reduced if not all the CdSe is consumed, and a 
remnant hexagonal n-type layer remains. 
In this study, we have used CL in STEM to show that the individual 
CdSe grains are highly photo-active following the cadmium chloride 
activation process. The grain boundaries are passivated to some degree 
by chlorine decoration in a similar way to cadmium telluride. CdSe is 
photo-inactive prior to the activation process. However, due to their 
very small grain size, the large number of grain boundaries causes severe 
carrier recombination in the remnant CdSe and in the adjacent CdSeTe 
intermediate layers. These observations are confirmed using electrical 
measurements. The CdSe remnant moves the position of the p-n junction 
in the device. A new p-n junction is formed between the n-type CdSe 
remnant and adjacent p-type CdSeTe intermediate layer. However, the 
small, grained nature of the n-type CdSe remnant and p-type interme-
diate CdSeTe layer causes parasitic absorption. This dramatically re-
duces the short circuit current density and the device efficiency. 
Therefore, the precursor CdSe thickness in the CdSe/CdTe stack must be 
precisely controlled to completely remove the CdSe remnant and elim-
inate the parasitic absorption. 
Interestingly, the band gap energy (1.7 eV) of CdSe and its high 
photo-activity make it a promising top cell in a silicon-based tandem 
photovoltaic device.
